opus-5.5.text:
I think they're quite remarkable, and as a physicist I find them very exciting, because power laws are exactly the kind of thing we're trained to look for. When you see a clean power law that holds over many orders of magnitude, in the number of parameters, the amount of data, or compute, it usually tells you that something general is going on. The details of the architecture or the optimizer don't matter that much, and there's some underlying principle controlling the behavior.

From a practical point of view, of course, their significance is enormous. They've essentially guided how the industry allocates resources: how big a model to train, how much data you need, how to trade one against the other. The fact that you can extrapolate performance before spending enormous amounts of compute is extremely valuable.

But scientifically, I think the most interesting thing is that we don't really understand where these exponents come from. Classical learning theory doesn't predict them. If you take the standard worst-case bounds, you get either exponents that are far too pessimistic, because of the curse of dimensionality, or generic rates that don't depend on the task at all. Empirically, though, the exponents do depend on the task. They're different for language, for images, and so on. That tells you the exponents encode something about the structure of the data.

So for me the key question is what property of real data makes it learnable with relatively few examples in very high dimension, and how that property sets the exponent. In our work we've been trying to approach this with simple generative models of data. One example is hierarchical, compositional models, a bit like a formal grammar, where high-level features are built from lower-level ones. In such models you can actually compute how many samples you need to learn the different levels of the hierarchy, and you see that learning proceeds step by step. With more data, the network can resolve correlations at larger and larger scales and builds increasingly abstract representations. A power-law learning curve can emerge from this progressive process.

So I see the scaling laws partly as an engineering tool, but mainly as an experimental fact that a theory of deep learning must explain. It's a bit like the role of scaling laws in critical phenomena in physics. They were first observed, and the real understanding came when people explained why the exponents are what they are and why they're universal. I think we're at the beginning of that process for deep learning.

r002.rationale: It says the exponents are not understood and discusses how performance follows power-law learning curves as data increases, including that exponents vary by task.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think they're very important observations, and they're also quite surprising from the point of view of a physicist. What Kaplan and his colleagues found is that if you look at the test error, or the loss, of these models and you plot it as a function of the amount of data, or the number of parameters, or the compute, you get a power law. And a power law is something that extends over many decades, so it's a very clean, very robust phenomenon. For a physicist, when you see a power law, the first thing you think is that there must be some hidden structure, some kind of scale invariance in the problem, and you want to understand where the exponent comes from.

Now, the reason it is surprising is that if you take the classical view from statistical learning theory, you would expect learning to be governed by the curse of dimensionality. The data live in very high dimensions, images or text, and if the task were generic, the error would decay with an exponent that goes like one over the dimension, so essentially it would not decay at all. Nothing would work. But empirically the exponents one measures are not small, they are of order a few tenths, sometimes larger, and they do not seem to depend on the nominal dimension of the input. So the scaling laws are really telling you that there is structure in the data that the networks are able to exploit, and that this structure is what governs how fast you learn.

So to me the significance is twofold. On the practical side, of course, it tells engineers how to allocate resources, how much data versus how much compute, and it gives this sense that things are predictable, which was not at all obvious a few years ago. But on the scientific side, I think it is a kind of experimental fact that any theory of deep learning has to explain. The exponent is a measurable quantity, like a critical exponent in a phase transition, and if your theory of what the network is learning cannot predict it, or at least relate it to properties of the data, then the theory is probably missing something essential.

In my own work, we have been trying to connect these exponents to specific properties of the data, for instance its hierarchical or compositional structure, or the fact that it lies near low-dimensional manifolds, or that the task is invariant to certain transformations. In simple settings you can actually compute the exponent, and you find that it depends on how the data are organized rather than on the dimension of the space. And what is interesting is that different architectures, say kernels versus networks that learn features, can give different exponents on the same data, which is a quantitative way of saying what feature learning buys you. So I view the scaling laws as a window into the structure of natural data, and into what these models are really doing when they learn.

astra-6.text:
I think the remarkable thing is that they suggest there is some regularity in a problem that looks extremely complicated. You have a very large neural network, a complicated dataset, and an optimization procedure, yet the loss changes in a fairly simple way as you increase resources. From a physicist’s perspective, that is very appealing: it suggests that there may be a relatively simple explanation underneath all this complexity.

But observing a scaling law and understanding it are two different things. What determines the exponent? Which properties of the data matter? Are you limited by the amount of data, the size of the model, or the computation used to train it? Different mechanisms can produce similar-looking curves, so the observation alone does not settle those questions.

There is also a practical significance: these regularities can help you decide how to allocate resources. Scientifically, though, I would see them as a starting point—a constraint that a theory of learning should explain—rather than a guarantee that the same trend will continue indefinitely.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the significance is that they turned something very complicated—the performance of a trained neural network—into something you can study quantitatively. You change the amount of data, the size of the model, or the computational budget, and you find surprisingly regular relationships. From a physicist’s perspective, that’s very exciting: it suggests there may be relatively simple principles underneath all these details.

But observing a scaling law and understanding it are different things. A power law alone doesn’t tell you which mechanism is responsible, or whether the same behavior will continue when you change the task or the distribution of data. So I see these observations as both a very useful practical guide and a challenge for theory. Can we explain where the exponents come from, what properties of the data matter, and where the scaling should break down?
